did_you_know.text: The word “kavod” can also mean wealth and property, not only honor or respect.
The expression “his face changed” describes a change in attitude or mood, not an actual change in his face.
“The land of your birth” means the homeland where you or your ancestors came from; here, it is Canaan.
“Ten times” is an expression meaning many times, not necessarily an exact count of ten.
“Spotted” animals had patches, while “streaked” animals had bands or rings of a different color.
Jacob recalls Bethel, where he dreamed of the ladder and made a vow after leaving Canaan.
In ancient times, camels carried people and goods on long journeys, making them especially valuable to wealthy families.
Teraphim were small household idols, probably connected with protection, divination, or family status.
The river Jacob crossed is usually identified as the Euphrates, which lay between Aram and Canaan.
The expression “from good to bad” means to speak about anything at all, whether favorable or unfavorable.
The tambourine and lyre were ancient instruments used for celebrations, singing, and dancing.
Jacob does not know that Rachel took the teraphim, so he makes a severe statement without knowing whom it might affect.
The “camel’s saddle” was probably a seat or basket placed on the camel, not an ordinary sleeping cushion.
“The way of women” is a polite expression for menstruation, a condition requiring special consideration in the ancient world.
The verse describes the hardships of a shepherd: intense heat by day, cold at night, and little sleep.
The twenty years of work were divided into fourteen years for Leah and Rachel and six years for the flocks.
Laban gives the mound an Aramaic name, “Jegar-sahadutha,” while Jacob gives it the Hebrew name “Gilead”; both names are connected with testimony.
“Mizpah” is related to the idea of watching or keeping guard; it describes a place from which one looks out over the distance.
